title: Leaks and RAII
learningGoals: explain what a memory leak is
see how a destructor cleans up

youtube.title: C++ Memory Leaks and RAII Explained | C++ Programming EP 48
youtube.description: In this episode you will explain what a memory leak is, explain RAII and see how a destructor cleans up, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 Leaks and RAII · 0:55 A destructor runs · 1:35 The life of a variable · 2:05 Second program · 3:05 Recap · 3:36 Bug of the Day · 4:24 Challenge · 4:44 Next episode

thumbnail.visual: big text "NO LEAKS" in tomato on lilac; Xecxec next to a leaking tap and a locked cupboard; thin black border and drop shadow.
thumbnail.pose: Xecxec next to a leaking tap and a locked cupboard

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Today we stop leaks for good. The trick is simple. Let a variable do the cleaning when it dies.

scenes.onScreen: "Leaks and RAII": numbered lines (1. A leak happens when memory is never freed; 2. RAII ties cleanup to a variable's life; 3. A destructor runs when the variable ends) and an analogy card: a hotel room that locks and cleans itself when you check out
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: A memory leak happens when you lose the address of a heap box before you free it. An early return or an error can cause it. The cure is RAII. It means that a resource belongs to a variable. When the variable dies, a special function called the destructor runs, and it frees the resource. Think of a hotel room. It cleans itself when you check out.
points: A leak happens when memory is never freed
RAII ties cleanup to a variable's life
A destructor runs when the variable ends

analogy.title: Leaks and RAII
analogy.body: A hotel room that locks and cleans itself when you check out

scenes.onScreen: raii.cpp: a struct prints a message when it is made and when it dies
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 4] This struct has two special functions. We study them in module six. [HL 5] The first runs when a Noisy is made. [HL 6] The second, with a tilde, runs when it dies. [HL 11] Here a Noisy is made, and open prints. [HL 12] Then working prints. [HL 14] The block ends, so n dies and close prints before the next line.

scenes.onScreen: a flow: made, used, closing brace, destructor runs
scenes.animation: Steps drop in left to right with a pop; connecting arrows draw on; the active step glows butter
scenes.narration: Follow the life of n. It is made, and open prints. The block uses it. At the closing brace, n goes out of scope. The destructor runs at once, and close prints. You did not write any cleanup call.

diagram.caption: a flow: made, used, closing brace, destructor runs

scenes.onScreen: leak.cpp: an early return skips the delete
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 10] This function makes a Noisy on the heap with new. [HL 11] If fail is true, the function returns early. [HL 14] The delete is skipped. [HL 18] The first call prints open and close. [HL 19] The second call prints open only. The close is missing. That box is leaked.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as leak dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. The program prints open, close, and then open. The last close is missing.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. A leak means that memory is never freed. Two. An early return can skip a delete. Three. RAII ties cleanup to the life of a variable. Four. The destructor runs when the variable goes out of scope. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: A leak means that memory is never freed.
An early return can skip a delete.
RAII ties cleanup to the life of a variable.
The destructor runs when the variable goes out of scope.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: A leak you cannot see
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; the program runs and the wrong output appears in tomato; the fix slides in and the output turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. The program prints open, but it never prints close. The early return skips the delete, so the destructor never runs. That is a leak. Use an ordinary local variable instead. Its destructor runs on every way out.

scenes.onScreen: My program had a leak. I tried to fix it with a bucket, but the bucket was on the heap.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw
scenes.narration: My program had a leak. I tried to fix it with a bucket, but the bucket was on the heap.

scenes.animation: Task card pops in; checklist ticks with a pop; Xecxec holds a tiny pen
scenes.narration: Your challenge: Write a function with new and two return statements. Show which return leaks. Then fix it with a local variable. Write your answer in the comments.

scenes.animation: Next-episode card slides up with a whoosh; right side stays empty for end-screen elements; sign-off text types in
scenes.narration: Next time: unique pointers. Keep coding, says Xecxec!

pun: "My program had a leak. I tried to fix it with a bucket, but the bucket was on the heap."
challenge: Write a function with new and two return statements. Show which return leaks. Then fix it with a local variable.
challengeAnswer: The return before the delete leaks. Replace the pointer with a local variable, and the destructor runs on both returns.
